content: Tension-type headache (TTH) is a common primary headache disorder characterized by a dull, non-pulsatile, diffuse pain that often feels like a band or vise around the head. The pain is typically mild to moderate in intensity and can affect the head, scalp, or neck. Subtypes of TTH are classified based on the frequency and severity of symptoms. While the exact cause remains unclear, TTH has been associated with muscle contraction and stress. The International Headache Society renamed this condition tension-type headache in 1988, and it is the most prevalent type of primary headache. The pathophysiology of TTH is multifactorial, involving increased sensitivity of central and peripheral nociceptive pathways, as well as genetic and environmental factors. Hypersensitivity of these pathways, lack of habituation, and the role of nitric oxide are thought to contribute to the condition. Despite these insights, the precise etiology of TTH remains unknown, and multiple pathophysiological mechanisms are believed to explain its potential causes. Differential diagnoses for TTH include migraine, cluster headache, and secondary headaches such as medication overuse headache, sinus headache, and cervicogenic headache. TTH is the most common type of headache globally and the second most prevalent disorder worldwide. It is more common in females than males, and limited data suggest a higher prevalence in white populations compared to black populations in the United States. The prevalence of TTH peaks in the fourth decade of life and decreases with age, as shown in studies such as those conducted in Denmark. Various precipitating factors can trigger TTH in susceptible individuals. Approximately half of TTH patients identify stress or hunger as triggers. Other common triggers include sleep deprivation, irregular meal times, eyestrain, alcohol, caffeine, colds, flu, sinus infections, dental problems (e.g., jaw clenching or teeth grinding), excessive smoking, fatigue, and overexertion. TTH is considered a lifelong condition with a significant socioeconomic impact. It often leads to reduced quality of life and functional disability. If left untreated or undiagnosed, TTH is associated with an increased risk of depression and suicide due to its profound impact on daily functioning. TTH that occurs as a symptom of another condition is typically relieved when the underlying condition is treated. However, frequent use of pain medications in TTH patients can lead to medication overuse headache. The diagnostic criteria for TTH are outlined in the International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3). TTH pain is often described as a constant pressure, as if the head is being squeezed in a vise. The pain is frequently bilateral, meaning it occurs on both sides of the head simultaneously. It is typically mild to moderate in intensity but can occasionally be severe. Unlike migraines, TTH pain does not worsen with physical activity. Physical examination findings in TTH may include increased tenderness in the pericranial muscles (head, neck, or shoulders) and myofascial tissue upon manual palpation. There may also be an increased number of myofascial trigger points in muscles such as the frontal, temporal, masseter, pterygoid, sternocleidomastoid, splenius, and trapezius muscles. Laboratory investigations, such as electrophysiologic testing (e.g., evoked potentials, electroencephalography) and cerebrospinal fluid analysis, are generally not helpful in diagnosing TTH and require further research for validation. Neuroimaging is typically not indicated for TTH patients unless there are abnormal neurological examination findings, atypical presentations, or presentations that do not meet ICHD-3 criteria. When neuroimaging is necessary, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without contrast is preferred over non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scans. MRI is often used to rule out underlying structural brain lesions or to evaluate the brain and pituitary gland in patients with features highly suspicious of TTH. Episodic TTH generally responds well to over-the-counter analgesics such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, or aspirin. Simple analgesic monotherapy with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or aspirin is recommended (Grade 1A) for treating episodic TTH. For patients who do not respond to simple analgesics, combination therapy with caffeine may be used (Grade 2A). However, combination therapies involving opioids or butalbital are not recommended as first-line agents for TTH treatment (Grade 1C). Severe TTH may require inpatient treatment with medications such as chlorpromazine, metoclopramide, a combination of metoclopramide and diphenhydramine, or intramuscular ketorolac. Preventive and prophylactic treatment is generally indicated for chronic TTH and frequent episodic TTH. Pharmacologic prevention options include tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (e.g., mirtazapine, venlafaxine), and anticonvulsants (e.g., gabapentin, topiramate). Behavioral treatments such as relaxation therapy, biofeedback, and cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) are also effective. For patients with frequent episodic or chronic TTH, combined therapy with tricyclic antidepressants and stress management is recommended over monotherapy with either approach alone (Grade 2B). For patients who prefer pharmacologic therapy, amitriptyline is recommended (Grade 2B). For those who do not require pharmacologic therapy, electromyography biofeedback combined with relaxation therapy is suggested (Grade 2B). Acupuncture (Grade 2B) or physical therapy (Grade 2C) may be considered for patients who cannot tolerate or require more effective treatments than amitriptyline and biofeedback. Historically, TTH was referred to as stress headache, tension headache, muscle-contraction headache, psychomyogenic headache, or psychogenic headache. The International Headache Society renamed it tension-type headache in 1988. TTH can be classified as episodic or chronic. Episodic TTH occurs less than 15 days per month, while chronic TTH occurs 15 or more days per month for at least six months. TTH episodes can last from minutes to days or even months, though a typical episode lasts 4–6 hours.
